newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel says coalition will survive tax turbulence.
newsitem.headline: Waigel says coalition will survive tax turbulence.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Monday that Bonn's coalition government would stick together until the next election and beyond despite the recent turbulence over surging budget deficits.

In a spirited and at times emotional defence of his ridiculed budgets, Waigel lashed out in a television interview at his critics both inside and outside the centre-right coalition that has appeared wobbly in recent weeks.

"This coalition will definitely hold together until the end of the legislative period," said Waigel, the leader of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) who was sharply attacked at the weekend by the centrist Free Democrats (FDP).

"With the similar views on environmental issues, economic issues and other issues, there are guarantees it will be able to rule for another legislative period as well," Waigel added. The next general elections are not due until late 1998.
The FDP at the weekend called Waigel's budget drafts a mass of juggled figures that changed every week.
"I do not just invent numbers," Waigel said, blaming unexpectedly weak economic growth for the budget shortfalls.
"I base my budgets on the economic growth rates the experts forecast. That is a realistic approach and it can be defended with a clear conscious."
He said the Bundesbank and the government's council of economic advisers had made forecasts in recent years that had overestimated economic growth, which led to lower tax revenues.
"Do you want to call the Bundesbank and the council of experts liars?" Waigel snapped. "I will not let myself be called a liar."

Waigel was especially pointed in his criticism of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), who with their majority in the upper house of parliament, the Bundesrat, have blocked some of his budget cutting measures.
"You cannot blame me when the consolidation efforts do not succeed after the SPD rejects the attempts to save," he said.
Waigel also bluntly told the FDP to cut out the criticism and stop acting as if it hadn't known about Germany's budget problems until it had to agree this month to putting off a planned tax cut.
"Herr Gerhardt and the FDP were all there when the budgets were put together," Waigel said, referring to FDP leader Wolfgang Gerhardt. "Nothing was put together in a vacuum.
